stem.en: Bhavisha and Dhruv each paid ₹1,000 at the end of every year into a scheme that pays 7% a year, and both stopped at age 65. Bhavisha started at 25 and paid in ₹40,000 in all; Dhruv started at 35 and paid in ₹30,000. At 65 Bhavisha has ₹1,99,635 and Dhruv has ₹94,461. Why is Dhruv's amount under half of hers, rather than about three quarters?

text.en: A smaller balance earns a lower rate of interest, so Dhruv's scheme paid him less each year than Bhavisha's scheme paid her.
Dhruv's last deposits had only a few years to grow, so his total should be 75% of hers and the printed amounts must be rounded.
Interest left in the account earns interest of its own, so Bhavisha's ten extra years worked on her earnings and not only on her deposits.
Bhavisha paid in ₹10,000 more than Dhruv, and that ₹10,000 alone, without any interest, makes up the ₹1,05,174 gap between them.

explanation.en: The rate is the same for both cousins, so the difference cannot come from a lower rate, and each of Dhruv's deposits really does earn less time than Bhavisha's. The size of the gap is what settles it: the two sets of deposits differ by ₹10,000, but the final amounts differ by ₹1,05,174. Only interest that stays in the account and earns interest itself can make a ₹10,000 difference in deposits turn into a ₹1,05,174 difference in the end amount. That is why ten extra years are worth more than the last ten deposits: they act on everything the account has already earned.

hints.en: Compare two numbers: the difference between their deposits, and the difference between their final amounts.
The deposits differ by ₹10,000. Work out ₹1,99,635 − ₹94,461 and see how far apart those two numbers are.
